column8: Welcome to Battles of History. This is not a battle. It is the background to the battles that follow. Between 1991 and 2014, Ukraine and Russia went from signing treaties that recognised each other's borders to an armed seizure of the parliament of Crimea. We will show you, slide by slide, what was signed, what was said, and what is still argued about. Some chapters describe deaths. We tell them plainly and without detail.

Ukraine and russia, 1991 to 2014. In 1991, the Soviet Union broke apart. Ukraine and Russia became independent neighbours, and promised to respect each other's borders. Over the next twenty-three years they settled many things, and argued about many others: nuclear weapons, Crimea, a fleet, gas, elections and alliances. The page ends with the armed seizure of Crimea's parliament, on the twenty-seventh of February 2014.

Where it is. Ukraine lies between Russia and the countries of central Europe, on the north coast of the Black Sea. In the south, the Crimean peninsula reaches into the Black Sea. Its port of seh-vas-to-pol was the home of a great naval fleet.

Who is who. Ukraine's presidents: Leonid krav-chook, Leonid kooch-ma, Viktor yoosh-chen-ko and Viktor ya-noo-ko-vich. Russia's presidents: Boris Yeltsin, Vladimir Putin and Dmitry med-ved-ev. On this page, Ukraine is red and Russia is blue.

How this page tells it. Each line is tagged with where it comes from. Some things are in signed documents. Some are only what one government said. Some were decided by courts. We tell you which. The two governments describe some of these events very differently. Where they do, we give both.

One country. For most of the twentieth century, Ukraine and Russia were two republics inside one state, the Soviet Union. In 1954, a Soviet decree moved the Crimean region from the Russian republic to the Ukrainian republic. The reasons given were economic and geographic ties. In May 1944, Stalin's government deported the Crimean Tatars, the peninsula's native Muslim people, from Crimea. From the late 1980s, they began to return. Ukraine's census of 2001 asked people their nationality. About three in four said Ukrainian, and about one in six Russian. In Crimea, most said Russian. That is not the same as the language people spoke at home, or how they voted.

Sovereignty. On the sixteenth of July 1990, Ukraine's parliament declared the republic's sovereignty. It said Ukraine intended to become a neutral state without nuclear weapons. That November, the Ukrainian and Russian republics signed a treaty. Each recognised the other's territorial integrity within the borders that then existed.

Independence. In August 1991, hard-liners tried to seize power in Moscow, and failed. On the twenty-fourth of August, Ukraine's parliament declared independence. On the first of December, the people voted. About ninety per cent said yes, on a turnout of eighty-four per cent. A majority voted yes in every region. About fifty-four per cent did so in Crimea, and fifty-seven per cent in seh-vas-to-pol, which was counted separately. In do-netsk and loo-hansk, about eighty-four per cent voted yes. Leonid krav-chook was elected president the same day. A week later, Russia, Ukraine and Belarus signed the agreement founding the Commonwealth of Independent States, and declared that the Soviet Union had ceased to exist. In it, they promised to respect each other's territorial integrity and existing borders. More republics joined them at al-ma a-ta. On Christmas Day, the Soviet leader, Mikhail Gorbachev, resigned.

The weapons. When the Soviet Union ended, about nineteen hundred strategic nuclear warheads were based in Ukraine, with a hundred and seventy-six long-range missiles and about forty-five heavy bombers. They were in Ukraine, but the authority to launch them stayed tied to Moscow. Ukraine agreed to give them up. In January 1994, in Moscow, the presidents of the United States, Russia and Ukraine agreed on the terms: fuel for Ukraine's nuclear power stations in return for the uranium in the warheads. In December 1994, at Budapest, Russia, the United States and Britain signed a memorandum with Ukraine, as Ukraine joined the treaty against the spread of nuclear weapons. They pledged to respect Ukraine's independence, sovereignty and existing borders, and to refrain from threatening or using force against its territorial integrity or political independence. These were assurances. They were not a promise to defend Ukraine with armies. The last trains carrying warheads arrived in Russia on the first of June 1996.

The Crimea question. Crimea had become an autonomous republic within Ukraine. Many of its leaders looked to Moscow. In May 1992, Crimea's parliament declared independence, on conditions, and planned a referendum. keev rejected it. Within weeks, Crimea's parliament revoked the declaration and shelved the referendum. In May 1992, Russia's parliament declared the Russian republic's 1954 decision on the transfer void. The following year, it claimed Russian federal status for seh-vas-to-pol. The UN Security Council, in a statement by its President, called that claim without effect. Yeltsin's government distanced itself from its parliament. In 1994, Crimeans elected Yuri mesh-kov, who wanted closer ties with Russia, as president of Crimea. In 1995, Ukraine's parliament abolished the post.

The fleet and the treaty. The Soviet Black Sea Fleet was based at seh-vas-to-pol. Both countries claimed it. In May 1997 they divided it. Russia took about four-fifths, and Ukraine about one-fifth. Russia leased bases in seh-vas-to-pol for twenty years. The rent was counted against Ukraine's debts to Russia. Days later, Presidents kooch-ma and Yeltsin signed a treaty of friendship. Each promised to respect the other's territorial integrity, and the inviolability of their borders. Both parliaments ratified it, and it came into force in 1999. In 2003, they signed a treaty on their land border.

kooch-ma and tooz-la. President kooch-ma built close economic ties with Russia, and also spoke of a "European choice". Ukraine joined nay-toe's Partnership for Peace in 1994. In 2000, the journalist gay-or-gee gon-gahd-zeh was murdered. Recordings made in kooch-ma's office led to protests. kooch-ma's part in it is still disputed. In the autumn of 2003, a Russian region began building a dam across the kerch Strait toward the small Ukrainian island of tooz-la. Ukraine sent border guards to the island. The building stopped after Presidents kooch-ma and Putin met. On Christmas Eve 2003, they signed a treaty treating the Sea of a-zov and the kerch Strait as internal waters of the two countries. They left the exact boundary for later agreement.

The Orange Revolution. In 2004, Viktor yoosh-chen-ko, of the opposition, ran for president against the prime minister, Viktor ya-noo-ko-vich, who was backed by President kooch-ma and supported by Moscow. During the campaign, yoosh-chen-ko was poisoned with dioxin. He survived. Who poisoned him has never been established. ya-noo-ko-vich was declared the winner of the runoff on the twenty-fourth of November. Election observers documented serious abuses. Large crowds gathered in keev, on Independence Square, the my-dahn, for weeks. Ukraine's Supreme Court ordered the runoff held again. yoosh-chen-ko won it. As part of the settlement, the constitution was changed to give parliament more power and the president less.

Gas. Ukraine was a major transit route for Russian gas to Europe. Ukraine bought Russian gas for itself too. On New Year's Day 2006, after an argument about price, Russia cut the supply of gas for Ukraine. A deal was made within days, through a company in between. On the first of January 2009, it happened again. By the seventh of January, Russian gas deliveries through Ukraine to Europe had stopped, in the middle of winter. The cutoff affected sixteen countries of the European Union, and Moldova. Deliveries resumed on the twentieth of January, under new ten-year contracts.

Bucharest and Georgia. In 2008, Ukraine's leaders asked to start the process of joining nay-toe. At Bucharest, nay-toe said Ukraine and Georgia "will become members of nay-toe". It gave no date and agreed to further talks. Neither country received a Membership Action Plan at the summit. A Russian newspaper, ko-mer-sahnt, later reported from an unnamed source that, in a closed meeting, President Putin told President Bush: "You understand, George, that Ukraine isn't even a state." We have no verified transcript for those words. After months of rising tensions, Georgian forces shelled tskin-vah-lee, in South o-see-sha, on the night of the seventh to the eighth of August. Russian forces then advanced deep into Georgia. Later that month, Russia recognised South o-see-sha and ab-kah-zee-a as independent. In Ukraine, opinion on nay-toe was divided. In a survey in 2009, more people opposed joining than supported it.

ya-noo-ko-vich. In 2010, Viktor ya-noo-ko-vich was elected president, with forty-nine per cent to Yulia tee-mo-shen-ko's forty-five and a half. International observers said the election met most standards. In April, at har-kiv, ya-noo-ko-vich and President med-ved-ev extended Russia's lease in seh-vas-to-pol by twenty-five more years, from 2017. In return, Ukraine got cheaper gas. That year, Ukraine's parliament declared the country non-aligned, outside military blocs. And Ukraine's Constitutional Court cancelled the 2004 changes, returning powers to the president. In 2011, Yulia tee-mo-shen-ko was sentenced to seven years in prison over the 2009 gas contracts. The European Union called it selective justice. In 2012, a new language law kept Ukrainian as the state language, and allowed regional or minority languages, such as Russian, to be used officially, generally where at least one in ten residents reported that language as their native language. ya-noo-ko-vich's government negotiated a far-reaching agreement with the European Union. The EU asked for reforms first, and an end to selective justice. Russia pressed Ukraine to join its customs union instead. In August 2013, Russian customs held up Ukrainian goods for about a week.

Euromaidan. On the twenty-first of November 2013, a week before the European summit at Vilnius, Ukraine's government suspended preparations to sign the agreement. That night, protesters gathered on the my-dahn. On the thirtieth of November, riot police violently cleared students from the square. The next day, a huge crowd filled central keev. On the seventeenth of December, Russia announced it would buy up to fifteen billion dollars of Ukrainian government bonds, and sell gas more cheaply. It bought the first three billion that month. In January, parliament passed laws restricting protest. There were clashes on hroo-shev-sko-ho Street. On the twenty-second of January, two protesters were shot dead. A third man died of his wounds three days later. Another protester was abducted and found dead. The laws were repealed, and the prime minister resigned.

February. On the eighteenth of February, three days of deadly violence began in central keev. That night, the Trade Union Building on the my-dahn, which the protesters had used as their headquarters, caught fire. On the twentieth of February, dozens of protesters were shot on in-stee-toot-ska Street. For the whole period of the my-dahn protests, the United Nations human rights office counts a hundred and eight protesters and others, and thirteen law-enforcement officers, killed. In 2023, a Ukrainian court convicted former riot police officers in connection with some of the shootings, and acquitted defendants on other charges. The verdict did not identify every shooter. On the twenty-first, ya-noo-ko-vich and the opposition leaders signed an agreement to restore the constitutional arrangements adopted in 2004, and to hold early elections. Russia's envoy did not sign. That night, ya-noo-ko-vich left keev. On the twenty-second, three hundred and twenty-eight members of parliament voted that ya-noo-ko-vich had withdrawn from his duties, and called an election for May. It was not the impeachment the constitution describes. On the twenty-third of February, parliament made its speaker, o-lek-sandr toor-chee-nov, acting president. It also voted to repeal the 2012 language law. The repeal was never signed into law. On the third of March, at the United Nations Security Council, Russia's representative, Vitaly choor-kin, called the change of power a coup.

The twenty-seventh of February. In a documentary preview shown in March 2015, President Putin said that on the night of the twenty-second to the twenty-third of February 2014 he told officials to start work on what he called returning Crimea to Russia. Early on the twenty-seventh of February 2014, armed men without insignia seized the parliament of Crimea, in sim-feh-ro-pol. At first, President Putin said these were local self-defence forces. On the seventeenth of April, Putin said Russian troops had stood behind Crimea's self-defence forces. The European Court of Human Rights later found that Russia exercised effective control over Crimea from the twenty-seventh of February, for the purposes of the European human rights convention. What happened next is told on the following pages: Crimea, and then the war in the Donbas.

Looking back. In 1991, Ukraine and Russia became independent, and in treaty after treaty promised to respect each other's borders. Ukraine gave up the nuclear weapons on its soil, in return for assurances. They divided the fleet, and Russia leased naval bases in seh-vas-to-pol. They argued about Crimea, gas, elections and alliances. After months of protests and deadly violence, President ya-noo-ko-vich left keev. Days later, armed men seized Crimea's parliament. Some historians, such as Richard sak-va, stress how nay-toe's growth eastward looked from Moscow, and Russia's sense of losing its place. Others, such as Serhii plo-hee, stress Ukraine's own choices as an independent country, and Russia's pressure and claims on it. Explaining why something happened is not the same as deciding who was responsible for each act. What the Budapest assurances obliged. In March 2014, Putin suggested that a revolution had created a new state, with which Russia had signed nothing. On the fifth of March, Ukraine, Britain and the United States said Russia was violating Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity, and called on Russia to consult with Ukraine under the memorandum. Whether February 2014 was a revolution or a coup. Who fired every shot on the my-dahn.

Between 1991 and 2014, Ukraine and Russia went from signing treaties that recognised each other's borders to an armed seizure of the parliament of Crimea. Over the next twenty-three years they settled many things, and argued about many others: nuclear weapons, Crimea, a fleet, gas, elections and alliances. The page ends with the armed seizure of Crimea's parliament, on the twenty-seventh of February 2014.

Where it is. Ukraine lies between Russia and the countries of central Europe, on the north coast of the Black Sea. In the south, the Crimean peninsula reaches into the Black Sea. Its port of seh-vas-to-pol was the home of a great naval fleet.

Who is who. Ukraine's presidents: Leonid krav-chook, Leonid kooch-ma, Viktor yoosh-chen-ko and Viktor ya-noo-ko-vich. Russia's presidents: Boris Yeltsin, Vladimir Putin and Dmitry med-ved-ev. On this page, Ukraine is red and Russia is blue.

How this page tells it. Each line is tagged with where it comes from. Some things are in signed documents. Some are only what one government said. Some were decided by courts. We tell you which. The two governments describe some of these events very differently. Where they do, we give both.

One country. For most of the twentieth century, Ukraine and Russia were two republics inside one state, the Soviet Union. In 1954, a Soviet decree moved the Crimean region from the Russian republic to the Ukrainian republic. The reasons given were economic and geographic ties. In May 1944, Stalin's government deported the Crimean Tatars, the peninsula's native Muslim people, from Crimea. From the late 1980s, they began to return. Ukraine's census of 2001 asked people their nationality. About three in four said Ukrainian, and about one in six Russian. In Crimea, most said Russian. That is not the same as the language people spoke at home, or how they voted.

Sovereignty. On the sixteenth of July 1990, Ukraine's parliament declared the republic's sovereignty. It said Ukraine intended to become a neutral state without nuclear weapons. That November, the Ukrainian and Russian republics signed a treaty. Each recognised the other's territorial integrity within the borders that then existed.

Independence. In August 1991, hard-liners tried to seize power in Moscow, and failed. On the twenty-fourth of August, Ukraine's parliament declared independence. On the first of December, the people voted. About ninety per cent said yes, on a turnout of eighty-four per cent. A majority voted yes in every region. About fifty-four per cent did so in Crimea, and fifty-seven per cent in seh-vas-to-pol, which was counted separately. In do-netsk and loo-hansk, about eighty-four per cent voted yes. Leonid krav-chook was elected president the same day. A week later, Russia, Ukraine and Belarus signed the agreement founding the Commonwealth of Independent States, and declared that the Soviet Union had ceased to exist. In it, they promised to respect each other's territorial integrity and existing borders. More republics joined them at al-ma a-ta. On Christmas Day, the Soviet leader, Mikhail Gorbachev, resigned.

The weapons. When the Soviet Union ended, about nineteen hundred strategic nuclear warheads were based in Ukraine, with a hundred and seventy-six long-range missiles and about forty-five heavy bombers. They were in Ukraine, but the authority to launch them stayed tied to Moscow. Ukraine agreed to give them up. In January 1994, in Moscow, the presidents of the United States, Russia and Ukraine agreed on the terms: fuel for Ukraine's nuclear power stations in return for the uranium in the warheads. They pledged to respect Ukraine's independence, sovereignty and existing borders, and to refrain from threatening or using force against its territorial integrity or political independence. These were assurances. They were not a promise to defend Ukraine with armies. The last trains carrying warheads arrived in Russia on the first of June 1996.
